summary:
Nizhny Novgorod Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender transition was banned outright in 2023 by the law signed by Vladimir Putin prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and the legal change of gender on official documents, and where gender-affirming care has been effectively banned since that year. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, and no discrimination protection is available to LGBT+ people. The Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, and the expanded "propaganda" law criminalises public expression including anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these laws face arrest, detention of up to 15 days, and deportation; the US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions by 30 June 2025 for alleged participation in the designated "international LGBT movement" or for displaying its alleged symbols, of which 98 were administrative and 3 criminal. At least 20 people faced criminal charges from January 2024 onward, and three publishing-house staff charged on 15 May 2025 face up to 12 years' imprisonment. Repeat display of banned symbols carries up to four years.

Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda statutes have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget across the two preceding years. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's designation ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly venues in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one bar were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night (The Guardian, 17 January 2024).

Physical coercion and death in custody are documented. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping. The Moscow Times (23 June 2025) reported arrests, club raids and extremism charges defining LGBTQ+ life through 2025, including a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the designation.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records these as country-wide conditions applying to this oblast, and states that no oblast-specific facts are documented. It assesses that LGB people are not generally at real risk of persecution solely on the basis of sexual orientation, while trans people, public LGBT+ advocates and people in the North Caucasus are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. The note also records that 139 people were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across the country between 2022 and 2024, and affirms that LGBT+ people constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
tangentialFactors:
Raids and extremism charges have so far concentrated in the largest cities: Moscow's LGBTQ-friendly bars and St Petersburg venues were the sites of the documented post-designation operations, which indicates the mechanism of enforcement rather than a regional limit on it. The oblast has no sourced record of its own raids, and the pattern is national.

Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia, and the UK Home Office standard is the operative benchmark for one of the main resettlement routes. The US State Department's Level 4 advisory is the corresponding warning for travel rather than emigration.

Counterpart figures suggest the enforcement apparatus is financially self-sustaining: propaganda-law fines alone contributed more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) to the state budget over two years, alongside eighteenfold growth in case volume across a decade.
localsOnly:
Residents of Nizhny Novgorod Oblast live under the same 2023 prohibition on legal gender recognition and the same effective ban on trans-specific healthcare; there is no lawful route for a resident to change gender markers on Russian documents or to obtain gender-affirming medical care.

Residents hold no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation, and the extremist designation exposes them to both administrative and criminal charges for possessing or displaying alleged symbols, with administrative cases accounting for 98 of the 101 convictions recorded to 30 June 2025.

Criminal exposure for residents includes up to four years for repeat display of banned symbols and up to 12 years for the most serious participation charges, as faced by the three publishing-house staff charged on 15 May 2025. Persons detained on extremism-related charges have died in pretrial detention.

Residents who seek to leave on refugee grounds are assessed under the UK standard, which treats LGBT+ people as a particular social group and identifies trans people as likely to face treatment amounting to persecution.
outOfScopeNotes:
No oblast-specific enforcement record is sourced for Nizhny Novgorod Oblast: the inventory contains no documented raids, prosecutions, or police actions in this oblast, and the UK Home Office note expressly states that no oblast-specific facts are documented. The country-wide findings are the only supported basis for expectation here.

The figure of 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 is not broken down by region or by gender identity in the source, so its application to this oblast cannot be established.

The conversion-therapy case documented by BBC Russian occurred near Novosibirsk; whether comparable forced treatment has been recorded in this oblast is unresolved and not sourced.

Whether oblast-level authorities in Nizhny Novgorod issue their own guidance on the propaganda or extremism statutes, or conduct separate inspections of venues, is not addressed by any source in this inventory.
